content:
Colleen Hoover's Verity is leaving theaters for living rooms this week. The psychological thriller starring Anne Hathaway, Dakota Johnson and Josh Hartnett opened in theaters on October 2, 2026, earned $162 million worldwide, and now heads to digital platforms for purchase and rental.

Timing depends on the clock: digital listings put the buy-and-rent debut at 9 p.m. PT on Monday, October 26, which is midnight ET on Tuesday, October 27, and other coverage dates the home release to October 27. What is clear is that this is a paid digital debut, not a free streaming launch: a free Prime Video streaming date has not been announced.

The story follows Lowen Ashleigh, a struggling writer played by Johnson, who is hired by Jeremy Crawford, played by Hartnett, to finish the book series of his wife, bestselling author Verity Crawford, played by Hathaway, after an accident leaves Verity unable to complete it. Moving into the Crawford home to work, Lowen finds what appears to be an unpublished manuscript with disturbing revelations about Verity, Jeremy and their family, and the line between fiction, manipulation and obsession begins to blur.

Michael Showalter directed the film from a screenplay by Nick Antosca, based on Hoover's 2018 novel. Ismael Cruz Córdova, Brady Wagner and Irina Dvorovenko co-star. The film runs about one hour and 57 minutes and is rated R.

Reception split sharply. Critics gave the film a 31 percent score on Rotten Tomatoes across 186 reviews, while audiences scored it at 72 percent. That gap is the story of its theatrical run: reviewers were cool, audiences were warmer, and the film still cleared $162 million worldwide.

Analysis: A Book-Club Movie Built for a Second Life at Home

A theatrical-to-digital window of just over three weeks says as much about the audience as the movie. Hoover adaptations travel on reader word of mouth, and a thriller built around a manuscript, a marriage and an unreliable truth is made to be paused, rewound and argued over at home. The critic-audience split also fits the pattern: this was never a critics' film, it was a readers' film, and the $162 million gross shows the readers showed up. The home debut is where that second conversation starts, and studios will be watching whether the same audience that carried it in theaters is willing to pay again to own the argument.
